uncited: This article defines the neural network architectures and data structures used to represent 3D scenes in differentiable volume rendering.

It solves the problem of mapping continuous 3D coordinates and viewing directions to radiance and density (or attenuation) values, enabling the synthesis of novel views from sparse or dense input imagery.

Unlike explicit voxel grids or mesh-based representations, these methods use coordinate-based networks (MLPs) or tensor decompositions to store scene information implicitly, allowing for high-frequency detail and differentiable optimization .
All methods in this family share the core mechanism of querying a neural network with 3D spatial coordinates $\mathbf{x}$ and a viewing direction $\mathbf{d}$ to predict scene properties.
**Coordinate Query:** The input to the representation is a 3D point $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3$.
In standard NeRF variants, the viewing direction $\mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ is also included to model view-dependent effects (specularity).
**Positional Encoding:** Raw coordinates are often mapped to higher dimensions using positional encoding $\gamma(\mathbf{x})$ to help the network learn high-frequency details .
**Volume Rendering:** The predicted values are integrated along rays using the volume rendering equation to produce pixel colors .
The concept of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) was introduced by Mildenhall et al. in 2020 .
This work established the paradigm of using MLPs to represent continuous 3D scenes for novel view synthesis.
Subsequent works, such as PixelNeRF (Yu et al., 2021), extended this to sparse-view settings by incorporating CNN-extracted features .
The Attenuation Field approach adapts this implicit representation for medical X-ray imaging, replacing the radiance model with the Beer–Lambert law .
